about.heading: WHO AM I
paragraphs: I build simulation tools and infrastructure and solve numerical modeling problems for engineering teams.

Long ago during my studies I was already building small numerical side projects. A symbolic circuit analysis tool, an eigenmode solver for the Schrödinger equation, a CUDA-accelerated 2D FDTD solver, a MIMO vector fitting implementation, and so on. I even wrote a 120-page LaTeX manuscript on linear system theory during the summer of 2021 to help out a friend.

paragraphs.text: During my master's I dipped my toes into the RFIC EDA world and worked on compact modeling and layout generation of RFIC passives (inductors, transformers, baluns...). This has now become RapidPassives, an open-source library.

At the beginning of my PhD (early 2023) I diverged from the circuit path to the more general system level, where you have signal flow diagrams and ODEs instead of Maxwell and KVL/KCL. During that time PathSim started as a side project. Initially just an analog computer emulator, it evolved into a fully fledged continuous and discrete (hybrid, we have events!) system modeling and simulation framework. I announced it in March 2025 as an open alternative to Simulink, and a modern take on system modeling in general. Clean API, mutability from the get-go, robust solvers (stiffness, algebraic loops, no problem). Today (mid 2026) we are at roughly 400 stars on GitHub and have many users and collaborators worldwide, some of them prominent figures such as the MIT Plasma Science and Fusion Center, scikit-rf, and JSBSim developers.

Now I'm making the full roundtrip back through circuits and fields, bringing it all together into one vertically integrated stack: EM solvers (RapidFEM, RapidMoM), a symbolic circuit engine (SANE), and system-level simulation (PathSim, FastSim). One architecture: SSA-style compute graphs at the heart of the engines, Rust cores, Python APIs, browser interfaces. The commercial EDA world splits these levels across vendors and decades of legacy. I think one coherent, modern stack can do better.

paragraphs: Those who have talked to me know that I can't stop talking about numerics, modeling, and simulation principles and ideas.

paragraphs.text: I work as a freelancer and license my tools commercially, free for academia. If you have something you want my take on, or need some ideas and even implementation, don't hesitate to reach out.

timeline.heading: one stack

body.text: The full roundtrip back through circuits and fields, built as one stack rather than six tools: RapidFEM and RapidMoM for electromagnetic fields, RapidMesh generating what they solve on, RSLAB underneath as the sparse direct solver, SANE for symbolic and numeric circuit analysis, FastSim compiling system models to native code.

body: One architecture throughout: SSA-style compute graphs at the heart of the engines, Rust cores, Python APIs, browser interfaces. The commercial EDA world splits these levels across vendors and decades of legacy; the bet is that one coherent stack does better.

It arrived in one run. RapidFEM and FastSim from April, then SANE, RSLAB, RapidMoM and RapidMesh from June, the fields, circuits and foundations levels growing together rather than in sequence, because a solver, its mesher and its linear algebra only fit if they are designed against each other.

Nothing in it is a wrapper. RSLAB took PARDISO's place and is benchmarked against it, RapidMesh took gmsh's, and both are validated against what they replaced. Owning the full depth is the slow way to build and the only way the layers actually fit.

timeline.heading: fusion

body.text: PathSim found users I never went looking for. The MIT Plasma Science and Fusion Center and the UK Atomic Energy Authority build tritium fuel-cycle models on it: a zero-dimensional residence-time model of an ARC-class power plant, a one-dimensional liquid-metal bubble column, and full FESTIM finite-element transport, all coupled inside one timestepping loop.

body: Mixing fidelities inside one model is exactly what the block-diagram abstraction is for. It took a fusion lab to prove the point: the same system model runs against lab experiments like BABY and LIBRA and against whole power-plant concepts, and a thirty-component bubbler transient solves in seconds, which is what makes uncertainty quantification affordable at all.

body.text: PathView came out of the same collaboration: it started at the Plasma Science and Fusion Center as a way to see PathSim models rather than read them. From November 2025 I rewrote it on my own stack and it moved to the PathSim organization, where it is now hosted free for everyone.

body: I presented the framework at the IAEA workshop on digital engineering for fusion energy in December 2025, and I am a co-author on the multi-fidelity fuel-cycle paper that came out of the collaboration.

timeline.heading: open source

body.text: The repository had been public since the summer of 2024, but March 2025 is when I actually announced PathSim: an open alternative to Simulink, with a clean API, mutability from the get-go, and solvers that handle stiffness and algebraic loops without ceremony. Published in the Journal of Open Source Software, released on PyPI and conda-forge, and picked up faster than I expected.

body: Past 400 stars and nine contributors later, the part I did not write is the interesting part: domain toolboxes for chemical engineering, batteries, vehicles, flight dynamics, RF and FMI co-simulation, several of them contributed by people I have never met. JSBSim picked it up for flight dynamics.

body.text: PathView followed: the same models as drag-and-drop block diagrams in the browser, running entirely client-side through Pyodide. Nothing to install to try it. PySimHub came out of the same year, a catalog for Python's scattered simulation communities, because the hard part of open source is being found.

From December 2024 I worked with Ralf Sommer, the inventor of Analog Insydes, on reviving that tool. Symbolic circuit analysis had been done properly once, in Mathematica, by people who knew exactly what they were doing, and then the industry moved on and left it there.
Picking those ideas back up on my own stack in June 2026 is what became SANE. Two years between reading someone else's design carefully and being able to rebuild it is about right.

timeline.heading: PathSim

body.text: Started in early 2023 at the beginning of the PhD as an analog computer emulator side project, PathSim grew into a full hybrid system modeling and simulation framework: custom solvers, an event system for discrete behaviour alongside continuous dynamics, and a block-diagram API built from first principles rather than copied from the tool everyone already had. It stayed on my own machine for a year and a half before the repository went public in the summer of 2024.

body: The same stretch brought three more: a minimalistic harmonic balance framework for nonlinear periodic steady-state response, a symbolic circuit analysis tool inspired by Analog Insydes, and a finite volume solver for quasi-electrostatic frequency-domain analysis that came out of the sensor modeling at the institute.

The solver needed a mesh, so it got one: a 2D QuadTree that refines toward edges and balances itself. Writing my own mesher for the first time is where the idea started that a solver and its mesher should be designed against each other, which is what RapidMesh is now.

timeline.heading: research associate, CMOS design
body: Research associate at the Institut fuer CMOS Design, TU Braunschweig. Three strands ran in parallel: numerical modeling of electrochemical sensors for analog circuit design, system design and hardware for bio-impedance spectroscopy, and an EDA pipeline for RFIC passives that was validated in silicon for cryogenic quantum applications.

body.text: That last one started as a Tkinter window that drew inductors and exported GDS. It became RapidPassives: browser-based layout generation with real-time preview and a WebGL viewer that renders million-polygon GDS at 60 fps. Six years of the same problem, and the tooling around it kept being the bottleneck.

timeline.heading: PhD candidate, TU Ilmenau
body: External PhD program in electrical engineering, run alongside the work in Braunschweig and everything that grew out of it.

timeline.heading: first repos
body: The first experiments that went public: an interactive 2D electromagnetic FDTD environment with a live field view, a fast relaxed vector fitting implementation that turns measured MIMO frequency responses into compact circuit models, and an interactive Bode plot tool for teaching.

Vector fitting had been sitting in a folder since 2020 as rational interpolation experiments, complex fitting by iteratively reweighted least squares, a stack of papers on passivity enforcement. Putting it on GitHub was mostly a decision to stop treating my own work as scratch files.

timeline.heading: things you could click
body: A run of interactive desktop toys, all pygame, all packaged with PyInstaller into a single executable so I could hand someone a file instead of an install guide. A Verlet physics sandbox with numba-compiled constraint solving, a few thousand particles on collision courses, and a random polygon generator built out of packed circles.

The one that mattered was the interactive Laplace domain: drag poles and zeros around the complex plane and watch magnitude, phase and step response follow in real time. Students got the pole-zero picture in a minute that a blackboard never delivered. Everything I have built since that runs in a browser is the same instinct with a better delivery mechanism.

timeline.heading: M.Sc. electrical engineering, TU Braunschweig
body: Master of science with honors, thesis graded excellent. Written at the Institut fuer CMOS Design between October 2022 and March 2023: area optimized neural network based modelling of passive magnetic structures for chip-level integration.

Three things had to be built for it. Polygonal windings parametrised down to the geometry, so a spiral inductor is a handful of numbers rather than a drawing. Infineon's B12HFC layerstack reduced to the layers an EM solver actually needs, because the full stack makes the simulation unaffordable. And a completely analytical derivation of the first and second partial derivatives of RLCk transfer functions with respect to the circuit parameters, read straight off the block structure of the MNA matrices.

body.text: Those derivative stencils are the idea SANE now runs symbolically over a whole compute graph, and the windings and layerstacks are what RapidPassives generates and RapidMoM solves. At the time I just wanted the optimizer to stop finite-differencing.

timeline.heading: research assistant, CMOS design
body: High-frequency measurement calibration methods, design and implementation of verification hardware, teaching the circuit theory seminar.

timeline.heading: writing it down
body: The 120-page LaTeX manuscript on linear system theory, written over the summer of 2021 to help out a friend: Laplace analysis, poles and zeros in the complex plane, frequency response, state space. It has since been translated to English and is still the clearest statement of the material everything after it rests on.

A separate writeup on state-space representations of linear time-invariant network models came first, in 2020. And for the tutorials I animated the parts that do not survive being drawn once on a blackboard: the rotating phasor, resonance sweeping through a Bode plot, the step response of a damped oscillator. Explaining things carefully turned out to be the same skill as designing an API.

timeline.heading: before GitHub
body: The first real project never made it to a repository. MiCir was a symbolic network analysis library written in Python from nothing: my own matrix class, my own complex arithmetic, my own polynomial and symbolic element types in s. Not because there was no numpy, but because I wanted to know what numpy was doing before I let it do it for me.

body.text: It read netlists, solved networks symbolically, synthesised Cauer ladders from a driving-point impedance, and drew its own Bode and locus plots. In February 2020 I typeset the whole thing in LaTeX, the first time I documented a tool of mine instead of just using it. It is the same problem SANE solves today, six years and a great deal of technique later: keep the circuit's symbolic structure instead of collapsing it into numbers, and read the answers off it.

body: The same folder holds the detours of a student with a compiler and time: Mandelbrot sets in the complex plane at resolutions my laptop resented, Monte Carlo estimates of pi, a DFT written out by hand to see where the symmetry comes from.

timeline.heading: internship, Volkswagen AG
body: Low-voltage and redundant power supply systems in Wolfsburg: concept, schematic, hardware, ASIL considerations.

timeline.heading: teaching assistant, TU Braunschweig
body: Weekly independent tutorials on linear dynamical systems and circuit theory for 50+ students, the material that became the throughline of everything since. Most of the tools above exist because a room full of people needed the same thing explained better.

The Fachschaft tutorial for Netzwerke / Wechselstroeme und Netzwerke came with its own problem set, typeset and drawn from scratch and never quite finished: networks with switching instants, initial values, asymptotic stability, harmonic steady state. Writing good exercises is the hardest form of understanding something.

timeline.heading: B.Sc. electrical engineering, TU Braunschweig
body: Bachelor of science, thesis graded excellent. Written over the winter of 2020/21: order reduction of interconnect network models for efficient calculation with SPICE simulators.

The interesting half was not the reduction but what has to survive it. A reduced RLC network model is only usable if it stays passive and stable, and both properties are readable off the structure of the MNA system matrices before any reduction happens. That is where I first met rational fitting, passivity enforcement and the papers that later became my vector fitting implementation.

timeline.heading: climbing coach, DAV Braunschweig
body: Led the competition climbing team from entry level to international level. First lesson in building things over years.

projects.heading: THE STACK
projects.intro: One vertically integrated simulation stack for electronics: from electromagnetic fields to circuits to systems. Open source where it builds trust, source-available and commercially licensed where it creates value. Free for academia.

items.heading: PathSim
paragraphs: A pure-Python framework for modeling and simulating dynamical systems. Built from first principles with custom solvers, an event system, and a modular block-diagram API.

Published in JOSS. Adopted by JSBSim for flight dynamics and used at MIT PSFC for nuclear fusion fuel-cycle modeling. Domain toolboxes for chemical engineering, batteries, vehicles, flight dynamics, RF, and FMI co-simulation, several of them community-contributed.
items.metrics: MIT open source / 30+ solvers / 9 contributors / PyPI + conda-forge

items.heading: FastSim
paragraphs: A drop-in Rust replacement for PathSim. Same Python API: swap the import and go. Python callbacks are traced into an SSA graph, symbolically differentiated, and compiled to native code at runtime.
items.metrics: 191x median per-step speedup (55-system benchmark catalog) / 21 ODE solvers / JIT + autodiff / FMI 3.0 / C99 code generation for embedded targets

items.heading: PathView
paragraphs: A browser-based visual editor for PathSim and FastSim models. Drag-and-drop block diagrams, live simulation preview, and instant sharing. Runs entirely in the browser via Pyodide, nothing to install.

items.heading: SANE
paragraphs: Symbolic Analog Network Engine: symbolic and numeric analog circuit analysis. One hash-consed symbolic DAG with automatic differentiation yields DC, transient, AC, poles/zeros, noise, harmonic balance, and exact first- and second-order parameter sensitivities. The graph preserves the circuit's symbolic structure and hierarchy and exploits it throughout.

SPICE and native Verilog-A frontends: compact models (BSIM, PSP, HICUM, ...) are lowered fully into the graph. Every parameter stays exposed to the autodiff, even in harmonic balance. Rust core, threaded sparse LU, optional JIT. Python API.
items.metrics: validated against ngspice & Xyce / scales past 100k parameters (IBM power-grid benchmarks)
items.statsText: try it live: sane.milanrother.com / core engine early access: info@milanrother.com

items.heading: RapidMoM
paragraphs: A 2.5D Method-of-Moments solver for planar RF passives on layered substrates (PCB, RFIC). Mixed-potential formulation, stable down to DC, layered-media Green's functions, and a fast ACA solver in O(N log N).
Zero-external-dependency pure Rust with a Python API: lightweight, installs in seconds, built for massive cloud parameter sweeps.
items.metrics: broadband S-parameters of an SG13G2 spiral via ROM sweep in ~5 s / ~600 MB / validated on the real IHP SG13G2 stack

items.heading: RapidFEM
paragraphs: Open-source Maxwell FEM solver in Rust with two backends behind one Python API: frequency-domain edge elements and time-domain discontinuous Galerkin. Scale-invariant from sub-micron RFIC to metre-scale antennas. Local notebook UI with interactive geometry, mesh, and field renderers.
items.metrics: pip install rapidfem / wheels for Windows, Linux, macOS / validated examples from microstrips to horn antennas

items.heading: RapidPassives
paragraphs: RFIC passive design tool. Browser-based layout generation with real-time preview, GDS export, and a custom instanced-WebGL viewer that renders million-polygon external GDS files at 60 fps.
items.metrics: SKY130, SG13G2, GF180MCU, ASAP7, FreePDK45 presets / fully client-side

groups.heading: foundations
groups.intro: The stack rests on its own numerical infrastructure. No black-box dependencies. Both are built for solver-in-the-loop operation: deterministic, budgetable, embeddable.

items.heading: RSLAB
paragraphs: A sparse direct solver for real and complex matrices, a PARDISO-style embeddable backend in pure Rust with no BLAS, LAPACK, or MKL dependency. Symmetric LDLT, unsymmetric LU, and a KLU path for circuit matrices, plus iterative solvers and preconditioners. Settings pick themselves: a deterministic heuristic (nested-dissection bakeoff, one-time hardware calibration), no ML in the default path. Mixed-precision solves come with an honest backward-error certificate, and peak memory and runtime are predicted exactly from the symbolic structure before any numeric work.
items.metrics: bit-identical across thread counts / faster than faer, ~5x to MKL PARDISO / PyPI

items.heading: RapidMesh
paragraphs: A 2D and 3D mesh generator for electromagnetic FEM and MoM in pure Rust. Exact-arithmetic CSG booleans, watertight by construction, count-based meshing with exact element budgets, and an API whose mesh representations serve the solver as an oracle. Replaces gmsh inside the stack.
items.metrics: exact CSG / dihedral-angle quality optimization / planar + tetrahedral

items.heading: SciData
paragraphs: A node-based environment for scientific data analysis. Drop a CSV, chain pandas, scipy, statsmodels and plotly blocks; the pipeline is a declarative graph that compiles to plain Python.

items.heading: ThesisOS
paragraphs: A local-first literature manager for researchers. Ingest PDFs, search them semantically, and trace citations across your library.
